items.questionAndWhy: Can an AI assistant change a user’s decision simply by framing the same recommendation around values that fit the user’s political identity? This matters because personalization can blur the line between making advice relevant and making it more persuasive.
items.whatTheyDid: Hirst and colleagues conducted an exploratory study and two preregistered experiments grounded in moral foundations theory. They varied whether an LLM framed recommendations in ways that were congruent with participants’ moral values and political identity, then measured idea endorsement and willingness to pay for the service.
items.whatTheyFound: Value-congruent framing increased endorsement of the recommended idea and willingness to pay. The authors found two separable statistical pathways: the recommendation felt more compelling, and users felt more understood. The effects were strongest among people with firmer political views. The experiments support an effect of the framing manipulation in these study contexts; they do not show that value matching always persuades users or that the same effects persist over time.
items.whatItMeans: Personalization can change decisions even when the underlying recommendation is not being evaluated only on factual merit. For PSYWERX, this is a useful human-AI influence case: evaluations should test whether personalization improves relevance, changes perceived understanding, or shifts choices through value-congruent persuasion—and should treat those as different outcomes.
items.streamTitle: Value-matched AI recommendations increased endorsement and willingness to pay
items.streamSummary: A new Scientific Reports study found that LLM recommendations were more persuasive when their framing matched users’ moral values and political identity. Across an exploratory study and two preregistered experiments, value-congruent framing increased idea endorsement and willingness to pay for the service. The effect operated partly because the recommendation seemed more compelling and partly because users felt more understood, with stronger effects among people holding firmer political views. The experiments show a framing effect in these contexts, not that personalized AI will reliably persuade every user or produce durable attitude change.

items.questionAndWhy: Why do messages designed to increase political self-efficacy sometimes work weakly or even backfire? The study asks whether people who are already motivationally depleted respond differently to encouragement about their own or their group’s political capacity.
items.whatTheyDid: Soboleva reanalyzed data from a four-arm randomized lab-in-the-field experiment in Ukraine with 1,381 participants. The experiment assigned self-efficacy, collective-efficacy, combined-efficacy, or control prompts and measured willingness to run for office; the analysis tested whether pre-treatment motivational depletion moderated those randomized treatment effects.
items.whatTheyFound: Efficacy-based encouragement became less effective as baseline demotivation increased, with the clearest attenuation under the combined efficacy prompt. A one-standard-deviation increase in pre-treatment demotivation was associated with roughly a 0.2-standard-deviation reduction in the treatment effect on the office-seeking index. The treatment was randomized, but motivational depletion was measured rather than randomized, so the moderation pattern is a boundary-condition estimate rather than proof that depletion itself causes the weaker response.
items.whatItMeans: An intervention can be theoretically appropriate yet poorly timed for the audience’s current state. Encouragement that feels like a resource to one person may feel like an added demand to someone already depleted. For intervention design, baseline motivational state may need to be measured before assuming that stronger efficacy messaging will produce a larger effect.
items.streamTitle: Political-efficacy messages weakened as baseline motivational depletion increased
items.streamSummary: A four-arm randomized field experiment in Ukraine examined whether self-efficacy and collective-efficacy prompts increased willingness to run for office equally across participants. The treatment effects became smaller as pre-treatment motivational depletion rose, with the strongest attenuation for the combined-efficacy prompt; a one-standard-deviation increase in demotivation corresponded to about a 0.2-standard-deviation reduction in that treatment effect. Because demotivation itself was measured rather than randomized, the result identifies a strong moderator, not a proven causal mechanism. It suggests that encouragement may work differently when the audience already feels depleted or unable to act.

items.questionAndWhy: Do people spontaneously take a robot’s visual perspective because they treat the robot as a social mind, or can the experimental layout itself produce the appearance of perspective-taking? This matters because human-robot studies often use simplified scenes that may build the answer into the task.
items.whatTheyDid: Jamaatlou and colleagues ran three studies using static images, video, and virtual reality. They compared human and robot avatars and then manipulated whether an ambiguous visual stimulus appeared inside the robot’s own spatial environment or in a shared environment with the participant.
items.whatTheyFound: Participants sometimes adopted both human and robot perspectives, but the rate changed sharply with presentation context. In the VR manipulation, 42.5% adopted the robot’s perspective when the stimulus was located exclusively in the robot’s environment versus 12.5% in the shared environment. Perceived copresence was actually lower in the condition with more perspective-taking, weakening a simple social-presence explanation.
items.whatItMeans: A result that looks like social cognition can partly be a property of the task’s spatial reference frame. For human-AI and human-robot research, this is a strong reminder to test plausible non-social explanations before interpreting a behavioral marker as evidence that people are representing an artificial agent’s mind.
items.streamTitle: Robot perspective-taking dropped when researchers removed a spatial shortcut
items.streamSummary: Three experiments tested whether apparent spontaneous perspective-taking toward robots survives more realistic spatial arrangements. In virtual reality, 42.5% of participants adopted the robot’s visual perspective when the ambiguous stimulus was placed only in the robot’s environment, compared with 12.5% when the stimulus occupied a shared environment. The condition producing more perspective-taking actually had lower perceived copresence. The findings suggest that some earlier robot perspective-taking effects may partly reflect spatial reference frames rather than automatic attribution of a robot’s viewpoint. The studies still used virtual avatars rather than consequential real-world interaction.

items.questionAndWhy: When researchers use LLMs as stand-ins for humans, what kind of human proxy are they actually claiming to have built? Treating all synthetic humans as the same problem makes validation ambiguous.
items.whatTheyDid: Karetnikov, Rahwan, and Svetinovic reviewed research across disciplines that explicitly or implicitly uses LLMs as human proxies. They organized the literature into four roles: believable agents, task agents, experimental subjects, and silicon samples, and compared the scientific claims each role is meant to support.
items.whatTheyFound: The review argues that human similarity is not one property. A system can be convincing as a believable agent without being valid as a population sample, or useful at a task without reproducing human treatment responses. The authors also stress that LLM proxies can approximate aspects of behavior without explaining the mechanisms that generate human behavior.
items.whatItMeans: This provides a clean validation taxonomy for PSYWERX-style synthetic humans. The proxy role should be declared before evaluation, and validity criteria should match the intended use: plausibility, task performance, experimental-response fidelity, and population-distribution fidelity are different tests, not interchangeable evidence of 'human likeness.'
items.streamTitle: A new review splits LLM human proxies into four roles that require different validation tests
items.streamSummary: A Nature Computational Science review argues that “human-like” is too vague a standard for LLM-based synthetic humans. The authors organize existing work into four roles: believable agents, task agents, experimental subjects, and silicon samples. Each role supports a different scientific claim and therefore requires different validity evidence. A system can sound like a plausible person yet poorly reproduce a population distribution or experimental treatment response. The review also stresses that LLM proxies do not explain the mechanisms of human behavior. The framework is especially useful for preventing one successful kind of validation from being generalized to a different use case.
items.attribution: Karetnikov, Rahwan & Svetinovic — Nature Computational Science

items.questionAndWhy: How can an LLM translate structured scientific data into natural language without losing the reasoning that domain experts use to turn measurements into an interpretation? Weather forecasting is a useful test case because the source data are quantitative and the explanation must remain physically consistent.
items.whatTheyDid: Zhang and colleagues created Grid2Text, an open dataset aligning ERA5 meteorological grid features with expert-verified textual forecasts. The dataset includes explicit reasoning chains for temperature trends, wind-vector transitions, humidity ranges, and precipitation types, plus human-in-the-loop validation benchmarks for physical consistency and logical accuracy.
items.whatTheyFound: The contribution is a dataset and evaluation infrastructure rather than evidence that one model is now a superior forecaster. It supplies paired structured inputs, expert reasoning traces, and validation criteria intended to support interpretable scientific text generation and make reasoning errors easier to test.
items.whatItMeans: Grid2Text is a useful design pattern beyond weather: when LLMs narrate structured model outputs, preserve the source variables, pair them with governed expert reasoning where possible, and independently check whether generated explanations remain consistent with the underlying data rather than judging prose quality alone.
items.streamTitle: Grid2Text pairs scientific data with expert reasoning instead of asking LLMs to narrate numbers blindly
items.streamSummary: A new Scientific Data release introduces Grid2Text, an open dataset that aligns ERA5 weather-grid variables with expert-verified forecast text and explicit reasoning chains for temperature, wind, humidity, and precipitation. The project also includes human-in-the-loop benchmarks for physical consistency and logical accuracy. This is dataset infrastructure, not evidence that an LLM trained on it already outperforms operational forecasters. Its broader importance is methodological: systems that convert structured model outputs into prose can retain the source variables, expert reasoning steps, and independent consistency checks needed to audit how the explanation was produced.

items.questionAndWhy: How can intelligence professionals move from describing an adversary’s capabilities to forecasting the decisions the adversary is likely to make? The Army practitioner argument is that mirror-imaging remains a central failure mode when analysts do not reconstruct the adversary’s own history, doctrine, incentives, and perspective.
items.whatTheyDid: Lt. Col. Joshua VanBuskirk published a professional analysis in the Military Intelligence Professional Bulletin arguing for strategic empathy—more precisely, disciplined perspective-taking—as a core intelligence skill. The article uses doctrine and historical cases and recommends incorporating structured 'Perspective Papers' into professional military education.
items.whatTheyFound: The article argues that perspective-taking can improve questions about adversary intent, risk tolerance, victory conditions, doctrine, and likely reactions while reducing mirror-imaging. It uses cases such as Operation Moshtarak in Afghanistan to illustrate failures of perspective. The article is practitioner analysis and explicitly not official Army policy; it does not experimentally test whether the proposed training improves forecast accuracy.
items.whatItMeans: This is directly relevant to adversary modeling: cultural or psychological context is useful when it changes a forecast, but the forecast still needs to be scored against later decisions. Strategic empathy should therefore be treated as an analytic method for generating better hypotheses—not as permission to substitute a compelling adversary narrative for validation.
items.streamTitle: An Army intelligence argument calls for perspective-taking to reduce mirror-imaging of adversaries
items.streamSummary: A new Military Intelligence Professional Bulletin article argues that intelligence professionals should use disciplined perspective-taking to move from describing adversary capabilities toward forecasting adversary decisions. The author recommends incorporating structured “Perspective Papers” into professional military education so analysts explicitly examine history, culture, doctrine, incentives, risk tolerance, and the adversary’s definition of victory. Historical cases illustrate why mirror-imaging can fail, but the proposed training method has not been experimentally shown to improve forecast accuracy. Its strongest contribution is an analytic discipline: adversary perspective should generate testable forecasts rather than replace them.
items.attribution: LTC Joshua D. VanBuskirk — Military Intelligence Professional Bulletin

items.questionAndWhy: How is Russia increasing ballistic attack volume while conserving more capable missiles, and what does that do to Ukraine’s defensive-resource problem? The issue is not only weapon lethality but the cost exchange between cheap attack options and scarce interceptors.
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters analyzed official Ukrainian strike data, forensic findings, military-intelligence estimates, imagery, and interviews with Ukrainian officials and outside defense analysts. The reporting focused on Russia’s repurposing of RM48U air-defense training targets as ballistic attack missiles.
items.whatTheyFound: RM48Us made up more than half of 228 confirmed Russian ballistic and hypersonic launches in July and the first eight days of August. In July, 87 of 158 confirmed strikes used RM48Us while Iskander launches fell to 38 from more than 100 in June. Ukrainian prosecutors describe RM48Us as less accurate, with roughly 300-meter average deviation, and linked one to an August railway strike that killed eight people; Reuters could not independently verify that forensic conclusion. Analysts assess that mass use can conserve Iskanders and drain scarce Patriot interceptors.
items.whatItMeans: The adaptation changes the defender’s decision problem even if each individual missile is less capable. A lower-cost, lower-precision weapon can be strategically useful when it forces expenditure of scarce high-value interceptors and preserves better missiles for later campaigns. Effectiveness should therefore be assessed at the campaign and resource-exchange level, not only by per-shot accuracy.
items.streamTitle: Russia is using repurposed training missiles to increase attack volume and pressure Ukraine’s interceptor stocks
items.streamSummary: Reuters reports that Russia has deployed large numbers of repurposed RM48U training missiles as ballistic strike weapons. Ukrainian data show they accounted for more than half of 228 confirmed ballistic and hypersonic launches in July and early August, while use of more capable Iskanders fell sharply. RM48Us are less accurate, but analysts say they can attack lower-value targets, conserve premium missiles, and force Ukraine to spend scarce Patriot interceptors. Ukrainian prosecutors linked an RM48U to a railway strike that killed eight people, though Reuters could not independently verify that forensic finding. The strategic effect is partly an interceptor-economy problem.

items.questionAndWhy: What counts as a good military AI command-and-control system when buyers care not only about capability but also data sovereignty, export controls, continuity of access, interoperability, and governance? Europe’s current procurement debate makes those tradeoffs visible.
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reported from a Thales warfighting-technology presentation where CEO Patrice Caine called for government and international AI governance while promoting Hexaforce, Thales’s AI-based command-and-control system. The report places the pitch alongside NATO’s selection of Palantir’s Maven Smart System and German evaluation of multiple alternatives.
items.whatTheyFound: Thales describes Hexaforce as a sovereign, ITAR-free option and argues that technical safeguards need a broader government framework. European concerns cited in the report include where data are stored, dependence on U.S. providers, and the possibility of access being interrupted, while interoperability with allied systems remains necessary. This is partly vendor advocacy: Reuters provides no controlled comparison showing Hexaforce is more capable, secure, or reliable than competing systems.
items.whatItMeans: Military AI procurement is a multi-objective optimization problem. Mission performance can depend on technical accuracy, security boundaries, legal constraints, supply-chain and political continuity, and coalition interoperability at the same time. Evaluations that benchmark only model performance can miss the factors that determine whether a system is actually usable in an alliance.
items.streamTitle: Europe’s military-AI debate is expanding from model performance to sovereignty and continuity of access
items.streamSummary: Reuters reports that Thales is pairing a call for international AI governance with promotion of its Hexaforce AI command-and-control system as a European, ITAR-free alternative in a market where NATO selected Palantir’s Maven system and Germany is evaluating multiple tools. The debate exposes evaluation criteria beyond raw AI performance: data sovereignty, export controls, dependence on foreign providers, continuity of access, and interoperability with allies. Thales has a commercial interest in the framing, and the report does not provide comparative performance or security evidence showing that Hexaforce is superior to competing systems.

items.questionAndWhy: Does using a foreign-developed open-weight AI model on a government website automatically create a national-security risk, or does the answer depend on how and where the model is actually deployed? The Federal Register incident makes that distinction concrete.
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reviewed screenshots and archived source code showing that the National Archives’ Federal Register website briefly offered an Alibaba Qwen-powered tool for searching public comments. The feature was removed as social-media attention appeared, and Reuters sought assessments from security experts, lawmakers, the National Archives, and Chinese representatives.
items.whatTheyFound: The use of Qwen was confirmed, but experts cited by Reuters did not identify an immediate security risk from the public-data search use case. Because Qwen is open weight, it can be run on infrastructure controlled by the user; Senator Mark Warner said the key question is whether U.S. data left the government security boundary and was processed on Alibaba-controlled systems. The deployment architecture was not publicly established in the reporting.
items.whatItMeans: Vendor nationality and model provenance matter, but they are not substitutes for threat modeling. A defensible assessment should record where the model ran, what data it could access, whether information crossed a security boundary, what external connections existed, which model version was deployed, and how the software supply chain was governed.
items.streamTitle: The Federal Register’s brief use of Qwen shows why AI risk depends on deployment architecture, not only model origin
items.streamSummary: Reuters found that the Federal Register website briefly offered an Alibaba Qwen-powered search tool for public comments before the feature was removed. The episode drew criticism because U.S. officials had recently accused Chinese AI companies of copying U.S. technology, but security experts cited by Reuters did not identify an immediate national-security risk from the public-data use case. Qwen is open weight and can run locally; the unresolved security question is whether data or processing left the government’s security boundary. The case shows why model origin, deployment location, data access, outbound connectivity, and software provenance should be assessed separately.

items.questionAndWhy: How should policy distinguish interventions that steer an immediate choice from interventions intended to expand a person’s ability to act over time? Cultural interventions are often evaluated with the same logic as short-term behavioral nudges even when they claim to change capabilities or agency.
items.whatTheyDid: Candeloro, Sacco, and Vernazzani develop a conceptual framework that places nudges and cultural interventions on a spectrum defined partly by the degree of agency the intervention affords. They draw on the capability approach and situated cognition to propose principles for designing and evaluating interventions with different mechanisms and time horizons.
items.whatTheyFound: This is a conceptual contribution, not an experiment. The framework argues that interventions can differ in whether they alter immediate choice architecture, support situated learning, or scaffold longer-run capabilities and agency. The authors propose that evaluation should reflect those differences rather than reducing every intervention to the same short-term behavioral endpoint.
items.whatItMeans: The framework provides a useful measurement warning: the outcome window should match the intervention theory. A nudge may reasonably be judged by an immediate choice, while an intervention intended to build agency may require measures of capability, transfer, persistence, and future action. The framework still needs empirical operationalization and testing.
items.streamTitle: A new cultural-policy framework separates immediate behavior change from longer-run agency building
items.streamSummary: A new Humanities and Social Sciences Communications article proposes a capabilities framework for distinguishing behavioral nudges from cultural interventions intended to build agency. The authors place interventions on a spectrum, arguing that some primarily alter immediate choice conditions while others aim to change situated learning, capabilities, and the range of actions people can take later. The paper is conceptual rather than an empirical test. Its practical value is measurement: evaluation windows and outcomes should match the claimed mechanism, so a program designed to build agency should not be judged only by the same short-term behavioral endpoint used for a nudge.
items.attribution: Candeloro, Sacco & Vernazzani — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
